New issue 76 by lewf...@gmail.com: beta(0.8,0.8) nearly always generates ~0
http://code.google.com/p/stan/issues/detail?id=76

What steps will reproduce the problem?

1) cd <stan-home>
2) make ../stan-test/beta-0.8
3) cd ../stan-test
4) ./beta-0.8 --samples="samples-0.8.csv"

What is the expected output? What do you see instead?

I expect the values for theta in samples-0.8.csv to be distributed
according to beta(0.8,0.8), approximately uniformly between 0 and 1, but
instead they are all tiny values close to zero (around 1e-16). This is
unexpected because this should be a very easy model to sample from.

Some other observations:

-Initializing theta to be 0.99 doesn't help.
-On a small fraction of runs, theta will be a reasonable value for a few
steps and then goes to a tiny value close to zero and stays there.
-When changing the model slightly to beta(1.0,1.0) the problem does not
seem to occur.

What version of the product are you using? On what operating system?
Stan 1.0.2
g++ (Ubuntu/Linaro 4.6.1-9ubuntu3) 4.6.1
Ubuntu 11.10
i686 32-bits
2gb RAM

Attachments:
beta-0.8.stan 88 bytes
samples-0.8.csv 29.6 KB

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: Issue 76 in stan: beta(0.8,0.8) nearly always generates ~0
parts: On 10/25/12 3:18 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:> You can go with a lot smaller of a guard at zero than e-15. In R,

>
> dbeta(1e-323,.8,.8,log=TRUE) # 148.3327
>
> but anything smaller overflows to Inf.

It didn't work at the original 1e-100 bound.

When Matt originally (I think it was Matt) put those
bounds in, he used 1 - 1e-15 for the upper bound and
1e-100 for the lower bound. The upper bound has to
be tighter because you can get closer to 0 with floating
point numbers than to 1.

The beta(x|0.8,0.8) turns into a function f(x) s.t.

f(x) = x^(0.8 - 1) * (1 - x)^(0.8 - 1)

log f(x) = -0.2 * (log x + log (1 - x))

d/dx log f(x) = -0.2 * ( 1 / x - 1 / (1 - x))

If x is very tiny or very close 1, big problems (pun
intended).

- Bob

Stan evaluates the log(beta(x|alpha,beta)) function just fine.
If you provide double-valued inputs, no gradient gets calculated,
and the result is the same as R's (it's a simple function, after
all).

If you use var inputs, you get the right value of the function,
but the gradients will overflow and HMC gets hosed.

Is there something you think we can make better here?

- Bob
